vignette:
A man in his 50s presented to the emergency department with 1 hour of acute, severe precordial chest pain radiating to his left arm, accompanied by sweating and nausea. Six hours prior, he had experienced similar chest pain at rest that resolved spontaneously after 30 minutes. Medical history included hypertension for 5 years, treated with reserpine.

Patient had diaphoresis and was in moderate distress. Vital signs: blood pressure 170/109 mm Hg, heart rate 87 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Jugular venous pressure was not elevated, lungs were clear. Heart sounds were regular and normal, without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Other physical examination findings were unremarkable.

Initial serum troponin I level: 1.159 ng/mL (normal range ≤0.028 ng/mL)

- ECG Findings:
First ECG (Figure A):
- Sinus rhythm of 67 beats per minute
- Upsloping ST-segment depression leads V1 through V6
- Tall, symmetric T waves in leads V2 and V3
- 2-mm ST-segment elevation in avR
- Reciprocal ST-segment depression in leads II, III, and aVF

Second ECG (Figure B):
- Upsloping ST-segment depression in leads V3 through V6
- Biphasic T waves in leads V2 to V4

- Coronary Angiography:
Revealed 95% stenosis of the proximal left anterior descending artery

- Echocardiography:
- Hypomotility in the anterior wall
- Left ventricular ejection fraction: 57%

Transbronchial needle aspiration of a right hilar mass showed benign bronchial cells. Somatic genetic analysis of cKIT and PDGFRA revealed no mutations, and germline testing was positive for NF1, suggesting wild-type GIST. Upper endoscopy and colonoscopy identified no other lesions. A 14-year-old girl presented to the emergency department with a worsening facial rash that began 6 days earlier. It initially appeared as red papules over the left cheek; her pediatrician prescribed acyclovir for presumed eczema herpeticum and instructed her to discontinue all topical products. Over the next 3 days, the rash progressed markedly, and she was brought to the hospital. 

Her medical history was notable only for a nonspecific facial rash of 2 years’ duration on both cheeks, diagnosed as atopic dermatitis and treated with triamcinolone 0.1% ointment twice daily. She had been applying this ointment to her face at least daily for 2 years, pausing for no more than 1–2 days at a time because the rash promptly returned.
